passage: I'm Gurleen, Kishore's cousin, and we grew up in the same building in Ludhiana. This year he applied to exactly one master's programme, in Milan. "Why waste fees on backups?" he said. "They'll take me." When his mother suggested two more colleges, he laughed. He even told his manager he'd be leaving in August and sold his old bike to a neighbour. I didn't say much. He sounded so sure, and I don't really know how admissions work. The email came on a Tuesday. Rejected. He didn't come down for dinner for two days. When I finally knocked, he said, "I never even thought about this happening." I don't know what he's planning now.

qa.a: Kishore applied to exactly one master's programme, in Milan.

Fest day: It poured from eleven. Half the crowd went home. The stall sold forty plates out of three hundred, and there was no freezer for the rest.
Three days later: Manoj sat on the hostel steps holding the stall's unpaid electricity bill. "If I'd even once imagined it going wrong," he said, "I'd have kept some money back. I never let myself think it."

passage: The hostel allotment list went up at six on a stormy evening, and Usha's name wasn't on it. She read it twice, rain dripping off the notice board's plastic cover. She had been so sure. "I'm in the top twenty of the batch, they always take the top twenty," she'd told everyone. So she had given notice on her rented room, which ended tomorrow. She hadn't looked at any other rooms. When Imran had asked, "What if the list is different this year?" she had laughed. Now her two bags were packed, the auto drivers weren't coming out in this rain, and she had nowhere to sleep tomorrow night. Imran found her under the canteen awning, staring at nothing. "I didn't even let myself think it could go wrong," she said. "That's why it feels like the floor fell." He handed her his umbrella. "Let's call your old landlord first."

passage: Last spring I applied to exactly one master's programme. Kamal, my friend from the lab, kept asking, "Jaya, where's your backup?" and I kept laughing. I had the grades, the professor's letter, the project. In my head I had already chosen a hostel room from the photos. I didn't write a single other application, and I told my parents not to worry. The rejection email came on a Tuesday at 3 p.m. I read it four times, sure it was a mistake. It wasn't. What hurt most wasn't only the no. It was that I had nowhere to put it. I had never let myself think "maybe," so the no landed on bare ground. This year I have a list of five, and a paragraph for each that starts, "If this fails..."

Hostel warden's note, Dharamshala, 22 September
Tenzin (second year) organised the class trek and was completely certain it would go well. When I asked about a rain plan, he said, "It won't rain, I've done this trail twice." He booked no shelter, packed no extra ponchos and told the group there was no need to check the forecast. Shalini, his co-organiser, suggested a later date as backup; he laughed it off. The storm came at noon. The group turned back, soaked, and two students' phones died. Tenzin came to my office in the evening and sat for a long time without speaking. Then he said, "I didn't even think it could go wrong." I stayed with him, and we listed what a backup plan would have needed. He asked if he could share the list with the class tomorrow.

qa.a: He felt shaken and ashamed, because he had never let himself imagine the trek going wrong, so the storm hit him harder.

qa.q: What did the warden do that helped, and what could Tenzin do next time?
qa.a: The warden stayed and listed what a backup plan would need; next time Tenzin could check the forecast and keep Shalini's later date ready.

qa.a: Shalini may feel frustrated that the backup date was laughed off, but also sorry for Tenzin.

passage: In Buenos Aires, Valentina was sure her band's first real gig would sell out. She booked the big hall downtown, not the small bar where they usually played. She paid the deposit from the money she'd saved for a trip. Felix, the drummer, said, "Maybe start smaller?" She laughed. "People love us. It'll be packed." She didn't plan what would happen if it wasn't. On the night, forty people came to a room built for four hundred. The echo made their songs sound thin. Valentina smiled on stage, but afterwards she sat in the empty hall, shaking. It wasn't only the money. She had been so certain that she'd never let herself imagine this. Felix sat beside her. "It's one night." "I know," she said. "It just feels like everything."

In the college placement cell, the notice listed thirty companies. Karthik had applied to one.

"Just one?" asked Gurleen, the student coordinator.

"It's the one. They'll pick me. My project is perfect for them, and the senior who interviewed there last year said I'm exactly their type."

"What if they don't?"

"They will." Karthik didn't even look at the list.

Gurleen found him sitting on the bench outside, very still. "I didn't make a backup," he said. "I never let myself even think about not getting it."

His voice cracked. It wasn't just the rejection. It was the shock of being wrong when he had been so sure.

Dear Chinmay,

You asked why I've been so quiet since March. Here's the honest version.

When Tanya, Sheetal and I decided to open a café in Pune, I was completely sure it would work. I left my internship for it. I didn't keep any other plan. When Papa asked, "And if it doesn't work?", I said, "It will." I actually got annoyed that he asked.

We had one location. When the landlord pulled out in February, we had nothing. Tanya went back to her job. Sheetal started her master's. I had quit everything.

I think what hurt most wasn't losing the café. It was that I'd never allowed myself to imagine losing it. So when it happened, I had no shock absorbers at all.

I'm applying for internships again. Next time I'll still dream big. But I'll keep a plan B in my pocket.

Your cousin,
Irawati

So you asked what the hardest thing about last year was, Zainab. Okay. I'm Sarika, and it was the breakup, but not how you think.

Dev and I had been together since first year. I was absolutely sure we'd get married. So sure, I turned down a master's seat in Delhi to stay in Chandigarh with him. I never even talked to my parents about the seat properly. When friends said, "Don't plan your whole life around one person," I rolled my eyes.

In October, he said he needed space. By December, it was over.

And it crushed me. Partly the loss. But mostly because I'd never allowed a single doubt in. There was no "what if" in my head at all.

I'm okay now. I've applied for that master's again. And I've learned something: you can believe in something and still keep a door open.
